steps.body: Back to fair shares — now with shapes. To split a shape into **fourths**, you cut it into four parts that are **equal in size**. The cuts can look different, but the pieces must cover the same amount. Unequal pieces aren't fourths, no matter how many there are.

widget.prompt: Each rectangle is cut into parts. Sort them: are the parts truly EQUAL (a fair split) or not?

items.label: Cut into 4 identical strips
items.feedback: Four matching strips — equal in size, a fair fourths split.

items.label: Cut into 1 big half and 2 small quarters
items.feedback: Three pieces of different sizes — not equal, so not thirds OR fourths.

items.label: Cut corner-to-corner into 2 matching triangles
items.feedback: Two triangles of the same size — a fair halves split.

items.label: Cut into 3 pieces where one is much bigger
items.feedback: One piece hogs the space — unequal, so these aren't real thirds.

widget.missFeedback: Fair means every piece is the same SIZE. Different-sized pieces aren't equal parts.
widget.successFeedback: Matching strips and matching triangles are fair; the lopsided cuts are not equal parts.

explanationVariants: Fourths must be four EQUAL parts — if one piece is bigger, the split fails, even with four pieces.
Counting four pieces isn't enough; a real fourths cut makes four same-size shares.

widget.prompt: A square is cut into 4 pieces, but one piece is clearly bigger than the others. Are these fourths?

options.label: No — fourths must be four EQUAL pieces
options.feedback: Four pieces, but unequal sizes — that fails the equal-parts rule. Not fourths.

options.label: Yes — there are four pieces
options.feedback: Counting to four isn't enough. Fourths must be equal in size, and one piece here is bigger.

options.label: Yes — any cut into 4 makes fourths
options.feedback: Only EQUAL cuts make fourths. Unequal pieces are just four pieces, not four fourths.

options.label: Only if the big piece is on top
options.feedback: Position doesn't matter — SIZE does. Since the pieces aren't equal, they aren't fourths.

steps.body: Surprise: equal parts don't have to be the same SHAPE — just the same amount. A square split by two lines into four small squares, or by an X into four triangles, both give fourths, because each piece covers a quarter of the area. **Equal area is the rule; matching shape is optional.**

explanationVariants: Both the four-squares cut and the X-into-triangles cut give pieces of equal area, so both are valid fourths.
Fourths care about equal SIZE, not identical shape — a triangle quarter counts as much as a square quarter.

widget.prompt: Square A is cut into 4 small squares. Square B (same size) is cut by an X into 4 triangles. Which shows fourths?

options.label: Both — each piece is a quarter of the area, even though the shapes differ
options.feedback: Equal area is what counts. Square-quarters and triangle-quarters are both valid fourths.

options.label: Only Square A — fourths must be square
options.feedback: Fourths don't have to be squares. The X makes four equal-area triangles — also fourths.

options.label: Only Square B — the X is the 'real' way
options.feedback: Both ways are real. The four small squares are equal-area too — equally valid fourths.

options.label: Neither — the pieces aren't identical
options.feedback: Pieces needn't be identical in shape, only equal in area. Both splits give true fourths.

widget.prompt: Tap every shape that is split into EQUAL parts (any shape of piece, as long as the sizes match).

hotspots.label: rectangle: 1 huge + 2 tiny
hotspots.feedback: The pieces are wildly different sizes — not an equal split.

hotspots.label: circle: 1 big slice + 3 slivers
hotspots.feedback: One big slice and three slivers — unequal, so not a fair split.

widget.missFeedback: Check the SIZES: equal parts means every piece covers the same amount, whatever its shape.
widget.successFeedback: The equal wedges, equal triangles, and equal strips are fair; the lopsided rectangle and pie are not.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents partition shapes.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for partition shapes must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines partition shapes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: The same whole cut into more equal parts makes each part smaller — eighths are smaller than fourths (the fractions sharing rule again).
More cuts, smaller pieces: splitting one pan into 8 gives thinner slices than splitting it into 4.

widget.prompt: You split one pan of brownies into fourths, then split an identical pan into eighths. Which pieces are bigger?

options.label: The fourths — fewer equal parts means bigger pieces
options.feedback: Same pan, fewer cuts, bigger shares. Fourths beat eighths — exactly the fraction sharing rule.

options.label: The eighths — 8 is more than 4
options.feedback: More parts means each is SMALLER, not bigger. Eighths split the same pan into thinner slices.

options.label: They're the same — same pan
options.feedback: Same pan, but different cut counts. More equal parts makes each part smaller: fourths win.

options.label: Can't tell without measuring
options.feedback: The rule settles it: more equal parts of one whole are always smaller. Fourths are bigger than eighths.

hints: Count the pieces AND check their sizes.
Six pieces, but are they all the same size?
Equal parts is about equal SIZE, not just the count.
explanationVariants: The cake has six pieces, but two are bigger than the rest — so they're NOT sixths. Sixths would need all six pieces equal in size. The judge rejects it.
Six unequal pieces fail the equal-parts rule; only six EQUAL pieces would be true sixths.

widget.prompt: A cake is cut into 6 pieces, but 2 of them are bigger than the other 4. Can the pieces be called sixths?

options.label: No — sixths must be six EQUAL pieces, and these aren't
options.feedback: Six pieces, but unequal sizes — that breaks the equal-parts rule. Not sixths.

options.label: Yes — there are six pieces
options.feedback: Six pieces alone isn't enough. Sixths must all be the same size, and two here are bigger.

options.label: Yes — cakes are always cut into sixths
options.feedback: Only EQUAL six-way cuts make sixths. Unequal pieces are just six pieces, not sixths.

options.label: Only the 4 small ones are sixths
options.feedback: A whole must be split into six EQUAL parts to have sixths — you can't mix sizes and name some of them sixths.

takeaways: Equal parts means equal SIZE — counting pieces isn't enough.
Pieces can differ in shape as long as their areas match.
More equal parts of one whole means smaller pieces.
steps.teaser: next: giving those equal parts their fraction names.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Fair means equal SIZE.** To make thirds, cut a shape into three pieces that each cover the same amount. Three pieces of different sizes aren't thirds — they're just three pieces. Same-size is the whole rule.

explanationVariants: Halves must be two equal pieces — unequal pieces aren't halves.
Two SAME-size pieces make halves; different sizes don't.

widget.prompt: A shape is cut into 2 pieces, but one is bigger. Are these halves?

options.label: No — halves must be two equal pieces
options.feedback: Unequal pieces aren't halves, even though there are two.

options.label: Yes — there are two pieces
options.feedback: Halves must be EQUAL. One bigger piece means these aren't halves.

options.label: Yes — any two pieces are halves
options.feedback: Only two EQUAL pieces are halves. These differ in size, so they aren't.
